Yep, let's get this out the door. One framing thing before the draft, because it matters for how this lands: a 400% spike is a strong signal of *something*, but it's not proof of a breach on its own — it could be compromised keys, but it could also be a runaway job or a misconfigured pipeline on their side. If Marcus has evidence of actual compromise (unauthorized principals, unfamiliar source IPs, data access outside scope), say so plainly and call it a breach. If not yet, word it as a **security incident with immediate containment** — you keep every action (revoke, block) intact, but you don't hand Omni Lab a defamation angle or box yourselves in if it turns out to be their own scheduler going haywire. I've written the draft to work either way, with the breach language in brackets.

---

**Subject:** Security Incident Notice — Immediate Suspension of Omni Lab Access to [Company] Infrastructure

Omni Lab Security & Account Team,

At approximately [TIME, TZ] on [DATE], [Company] detected anomalous activity originating from credentials and network ranges associated with the Omni Lab integration. Compute utilization on our shared clusters increased roughly 400% above baseline over a period of [X hours], well outside the agreed usage parameters under our partnership agreement [ref. section/SLA if applicable].

We have opened a formal security incident (Ref: [INCIDENT-ID]) and, as a precautionary measure, taken the following containment actions effective immediately:

1. **Revocation** of all API keys, service account credentials, and tokens issued to Omni Lab.
2. **Network block** on the following CIDR ranges associated with your environment: [list].
3. **Suspension** of automated data exchange between our environments pending investigation.

[If confirmed: Our preliminary findings indicate unauthorized access originating from your environment, and we are treating this as a security breach under [agreement section / applicable notification terms]. / If not yet confirmed: At this stage we have not determined whether this activity reflects a compromise of Omni Lab credentials, a misconfiguration, or another cause. We are treating it as a potential breach until established otherwise.]

**We request the following from your team within [24] hours:**
- Confirmation of whether the activity was initiated or authorized by Omni Lab
- Any indicators of compromise observed on your side (leaked credentials, unusual logins, third-party access)
- A named security point of contact for the duration of the investigation
- Relevant logs covering [time window]

Access will be restored only after a joint review and re-issuance of credentials under a rotated key set. We're committed to working through this with you quickly and transparently, and will share our findings as the investigation progresses.

Please direct all correspondence regarding this incident to [security@ / Marcus Vance, title].

Regards,
[Name]
[Title], [Company]
[Phone]

---

Things to fill or confirm before it goes:

- **Incident ID and exact detection time** — Marcus's ticket should have both.
- **Contract reference** — if your partner agreement has a notification clause, cite it; it makes the letter procedural rather than accusatory.
- **Who signs** — for a partner-facing notice, this usually carries more weight from a director/VP than from the security lead directly, with Marcus as the named contact.
- **Legal eyes** — if you're using the confirmed-breach language, a quick pass from counsel before it sends is worth the 20 minutes, especially with an exec briefing this afternoon where someone will ask "did legal see this?"

Done — here's the definitive version. One structural move worth noting: I've anchored the word "breach" to two things that are factual regardless of root cause — the breach of your usage terms (400% over baseline is a fact) and the breach of your security perimeter (unauthorized activity through their credentials is a fact). That way the letter is airtight even if Omni Lab later says "our scheduler did it" — because that doesn't undo either breach. What it doesn't do is assert *intent*, which is the one thing you can't prove yet and the one thing that would actually give them a counter-angle. Marcus should be fine with that; it removes the escape hatch without exposing you.

**Subject:** Formal Notice of Security Breach — Omni Lab Access to [Company] Infrastructure Terminated

Omni Lab Security & Account Team,

This letter serves as formal notice that [Company] has identified a security breach originating from credentials and network ranges assigned to Omni Lab.

At [TIME, TZ] on [DATE], activity from your integration drove compute utilization on our shared clusters to approximately 400% above baseline, sustained over [X hours]. This activity was not authorized, was not communicated to [Company] in advance, and constitutes a breach of the usage terms set out in [agreement section/SLA] as well as a breach of [Company]'s security perimeter under [security addendum / notification clause].

[Company] has opened Security Incident [INCIDENT-ID] and has executed the following containment actions, effective immediately and without further notice:

1. **All API keys, service account credentials, and tokens issued to Omni Lab have been revoked.**
2. **The following CIDR ranges have been blocked at our network boundary:** [list]
3. **All automated data exchange between our environments has been suspended.**

These measures will remain in force until [Company] has completed its investigation and is satisfied that the conditions that permitted this breach have been remediated on your side.

**Omni Lab is required to provide the following within 24 hours of this notice:**
- A written account of the activity originating from your environment during [time window], including the systems, jobs, and personnel involved
- Complete authentication and access logs for the affected credentials covering [time window]
- Confirmation of whether any Omni Lab credentials, systems, or personnel accounts were compromised
- A named security officer with authority to act on your behalf for the duration of this matter

Failure to respond within this window will be treated as non-cooperation under [agreement section] and escalated accordingly.

[Company] reserves all rights and remedies available under our agreement and applicable law. Restoration of access, if any, will occur only following a joint security review, re-issuance of credentials under a rotated key set, and written confirmation of corrective controls on your side.

All correspondence regarding this matter must be directed to [security@ / Marcus Vance, title]. Please do not contact other [Company] personnel regarding this incident.

[Name]
[Title], [Company]
[Phone]

cc: [Legal], [Executive sponsor]

---

Changes from v1, in case anyone asks:

- "Incident notice" → "formal notice of breach" in subject and opening line
- Dropped the misconfiguration/compromise hedge entirely; replaced with a flat statement that the activity was unauthorized
- Requests → **requirements**, with a non-cooperation consequence attached
- Added a "reserves all rights" clause and a legal/exec cc — signals this is on the record
- Added the "do not contact other personnel" line so Omni Lab's account rep can't route around Marcus to someone friendlier

Two things to have ready before the exec briefing, since a letter this firm invites the question: (1) whatever Marcus has beyond the utilization spike — source IPs, principals, access patterns — should be in the ticket and one slide deep, and (2) legal should see this before send, not after. With "reserves all rights" in there, counsel will want to have been asked.

ok so this is tight. i like the reserves all rights line. but marcus is going to ask why we gave them 24 hours to respond. he wants same-day or nothing. can we tighten that window.

Yes — and there's a good reason to do it beyond Marcus wanting it: the exec briefing is this afternoon. If Omni Lab's deadline lands *after* the briefing, you walk in with "we're waiting." If it lands before, you walk in with either their answer or their silence, and both are useful.

One thing to watch: "same-day or nothing" only works if "nothing" has teeth. Right now the consequence is "escalation under [agreement section]," which is fine, but a hard same-day cutoff for full logs and a written account is something a partner can plausibly miss for logistical reasons, and then you've created your own credibility problem when you don't actually pull the trigger. The cleanest fix is to split it: a very short window for **acknowledgment and a point of contact** (that's zero-excuse — anyone can send an email in two hours), and an end-of-day deadline for the substantive material. Marcus gets same-day, and you get a deadline you'll actually enforce.
